We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.

title: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
authors: Niyazi Ahmet Metin, Dilara Kek\"ull\"uo\u{g}lu
abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.

title: Let the Mind Conceive, Let the Hand Achieve: Coupling Grounded Action and Progress Evaluation for Long-Horizon Manipulation
authors: Youpeng Wen, Gang Wang, Tianyu Huang, Weiwei Zhang, Zhijian Huang, Wei Chen, Xieyuanli Chen, Yunhui Liu
abstract: A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation. Orchestra decomposes a complete multimodal instruction into ordered subtasks, tracks completed steps, and updates the locations of relevant objects and destinations during execution. It maintains a shared context containing the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations. An action policy uses this context to generate actions, while a separately trained progress evaluator estimates when to advance to the next subtask. To evaluate whether robots trained on atomic instructions and short trajectories can execute longer subtask sequences, we introduce a benchmark named RMBench-Compose. Orchestra achieves a mean success rate of $68.22\%$ across nine RMBench tasks, outperforming Mem-0 by $26.22$ percentage points. On RMBench-Compose, it achieves an Average Success Length (ASL) of $7.35$ subtasks, $2.46$ times that of HarnessVLA. Across four real-world multi-step tasks, it improves mean ASL by $25.0\%$ over Orchestra using the base $\pi_{0.5}$ policy. These results show that Orchestra helps robots carry out longer sequences of subtasks while preserving the requested subtask order and acting on the specified objects. Our code and project page are available at https://youpengwen.github.io/Orchestra

title: AdaRSI: On-Demand Recursive Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
authors: Peidong Wang, Ying Chang, Zhiming Ma, Lirong Che, Zihao Liu, Xiaocui Yang, Shi Feng, Daqi Liu, Yuzhe Yang, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Jian Su, Daling Wang
abstract: Failures in long-horizon embodied tasks can arise from how a vision-language-action model (VLA) is called or from its execution capabilities. We introduce AdaRSI, an on-demand recursive self-improvement framework in which a coding agent first refines its tools and procedures, then adapts sub-steps that remain unreliable after testing alternative instructions and approaches. The agent collects demonstrations, tests their utility through temporary fine-tuning probes, and pools accepted data across tasks to train a specialist VLA that works alongside the original executor. At the end of each development round, its records are summarized into shared experience that guides subsequent diagnosis and data collection. On unseen composite tasks in RoboCasa365, AdaRSI raises success from 4.6% to 13.3%. On perturbed LIBERO-Pro 2.0 tasks, success rises from 32.9% to 49.1%. On RoboCasa365's Composite-Unseen suite, it achieves higher success than adapting every manipulation sub-step, using 34% of the GPU time and 36% of the demonstrations. On a real robot, the agent autonomously collects demonstrations and adapts the executor to recover fallen bottles, improving task completion.

title: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
authors: Zhengxin Zhang, Maosen Tang, Ning Wang, Changhao Li, Jingren Zhou, Bo Dai, Sainyam Galhotra, Alex Townsend, Claire Cardie
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts, but generating complete rollouts and computing per-token teacher feedback are computationally expensive. Existing truncation methods save computation by stopping rollouts early. However, they do not compensate for truncated token gradients, which biases the gradient estimates and changes Vanilla OPD's original training objective. Furthermore, their truncation decisions rely on assumptions about supervision quality or criteria that may not generalize across settings. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.

title: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems?
authors: Jingyu Tang, Xu Yang, Zhehao Zhang, Zheng Wang, Qi Cheng, Haozhe Zhao, Manling Li, Wenxuan Li, Xide Xia, Jiaxin Pei
abstract: Real-time interaction requires agents to perceive evolving environments and act under temporal constraints, yet existing evaluations of real-time streaming models focus on conversational quality and streaming perception, leaving effective action under strict temporal constraints untested. We introduce Realtime-Bench, a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success. Under Wall Clock, where environments advance according to actual inference latency, the best success rate reaches only 44% and the best Pass^3 is only 36%, demonstrating that real-time interaction remains challenging. To separate serving latency from models' real-time streaming capability, we compare Wall Clock with Paused Clock, which removes inference delays as an idealized reference, and introduce Token Clock, which advances simulated time according to generated token counts, testing temporal awareness independently of physical serving speed. We find that temporal costs limit success in evolving environments and that higher reasoning effort has mixed effects under time pressure, reflecting a trade-off between decision quality and timely execution. Based on these results, we discuss future directions for improving real-time multimodal models, including adaptive reasoning with temporal awareness and continuous perception and action.

title: Agentic In-Context Learning: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn in Closed-Loop Interaction?
authors: Shiguang Wu, Yaqing Wang, Quanming Yao
abstract: The learning algorithm view of in-context learning (ICL) studies how fixed-parameter Transformers learn from supplied examples. Language model agents extend this setting through interaction: their actions determine what evidence enters context next. We call this regime Agentic In-Context Learning (Agentic ICL). Existing studies largely depend on externally supplied contexts or reward-bearing interaction histories, while work on general tool-using agents lacks a learning algorithm view. We represent an interactive learner by its state, update, and decision rule, covering active learning, bandits, and online reinforcement learning (RL). For expressivity, we construct causal Transformers that approximate these algorithms over a finite horizon, and bound the resulting loss in return. For training, we characterize when optimizing process rewards preserves behavior that maximizes the final outcome. Distillation experiments show that Transformers can learn to execute three representative recursions. We then train models from outcome or process rewards without oracle action or state targets, as in RL post-training. Different rewards yield distinct decision policies. Improving the alignment of process supervision with outcome-optimal action preferences shifts learned decisions accordingly. Such behavioral differences persist in a pretrained language model across textual paraphrases.

title: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
authors: Peter Racioppo
abstract: Self-attention encodes where a past token lies, but not how its uncertainty grows with time: evidence accumulates without bound as the context grows, and nothing indicates which tokens are safe to discard. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state governed by a stochastic differential equation. Under this model, each head draws bounded evidence from any context. This lets each head abstain when relevant evidence is weak, and gives each head a memory window outside which discarding tokens changes its output by a provably bounded amount. On language modeling, DKA outperforms RoPE within the training length and ALiBi far beyond it, and matches sliding-window attention with a substantially smaller key-value cache.

title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
authors: Shuyang Xiang
abstract: A black hole retains only a few conserved charges of the matter it formed from. We are inspired to make the analogy and we ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. For two prompts followed by the same continuation, the difference of their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-\alpha}$, where $\alpha=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks. Beyond the first layers, trained models forget faster ($\alpha\approx0.55$--$0.7$) than untrained ones of the same architecture ($\alpha\approx0.2$--$0.5$). For finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits and non-degenerate pre-norm activations, we prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for prompt length $P$ and depth $L$: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} through continuation tokens adds only logarithmic factors. Conditional on the generated text, the prompt's influence on the next token thus vanishes. The bound fixes only the asymptotic shape and is uninformative at the lengths we measure in trained networks; an exactly solvable linear relay model shows that it cannot be improved and accounts for the untrained curves. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias on the prompt stops the decay early in training, and training suppresses relay by about one billion tokens, before attention sinks form. A toolkit that measures $\alpha$ for any Hugging Face causal language model is publicly available.

title: Screening LLM Judges Without Ground Truth: A Preliminary Evaluation of an AI Dental Hygiene Coach
authors: William DeShong, Barath Kannan, Auberon Palma, Brenda Bradshaw, Ann Bruhn, James F. Leathrum, Jr., Yuzhong Shen
abstract: Evaluating a fine-tuned coaching model with expert graders is slow and expensive, and an LLM judge cannot be trusted without ground truth. We present a staged pipeline that screens candidate LLM judges and student models before expert review, using explicit decision rules at each stage: judge output audit, similarity with hosted judges, bias checks, and decision robustness. We demonstrate it on an AI dental hygiene coach. The case study uses synthetic, clinically unvalidated training and reference data to demonstrate the operation of the pipeline, rather than to establish the clinical performance of the resulting models. Two fine-tuned small language models (Granite-4.1-8B and Qwen3-8B), each trained at three data sizes, were scored on seven metrics by five judges (three local, two hosted). Two local judges, Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, were not distinguishable from the agreement between the hosted judges on six of seven metrics by rank correlation, and Qwen3.8-27B was the most similar to the hosted judges overall. No judge met our criterion for favoring its own model family or training-data source. The student comparison did not separate the two models on any metric under the pipeline's rule, so the choice of Granite-4.1-8B, which led in 29 of 35 judge-by-metric cells, is a lean that depends partly on truncated Qwen3-8B outputs. The pipeline also surfaced problems that raw scores hid, including the truncated outputs and hallucination flags from one hosted judge that no other judge corroborated. No dental hygiene expert has graded these responses, so the findings are preliminary and the pipeline's final stage, anchoring to expert judgement, is proposed but not performed.

title: Forecasting Retail Sales at Every Grain: Trees, Foundation Models, Transformers and World Models Compared on Four Public Data Sets
authors: Karthik Iyer, Madan Dabbeeru
abstract: A retailer makes decisions from the same demand at different grains: store orders by item and day, promotions by item and week, category reviews and supplier terms. This paper asks whether one forecast, built at the finest grain and summed to every coarser grain, can serve them all, and which model does that best. It compares LightGBM, pretrained foundation models (TimesFM, Chronos-Bolt, Timestral), the Temporal Fusion Transformer and a world model that carries each item's state forward under the price and promotion plan, on M5, six Dominick's categories, Breakfast at the Frat and Corporacion Favorita, with the world model and LightGBM tuned by a common search. When to use the average: the average of the tuned world model and LightGBM, summed to every grain, has the lowest error in 22 of 27 grain and data set cases and is never the least accurate on the final held-out periods. When to use the world model: on existing items kept out of training it loses at most 0.040 in scaled error, against up to 0.311 for LightGBM, and on lines with short history it is clearly more accurate on six of nine data sets. When to use LightGBM: on heavily promoted lines, fast sellers and lines with long history (six of nine data sets each) and in price-cut weeks. Inconclusive: lines never promoted and slow lines are close to even, and 52 weeks ahead the average is the most accurate on five of seven data sets, with the world model ahead of LightGBM on two of seven. The findings hold for these data sets and the price and promotion levers; anyone adopting them should rerun every comparison on their own data.

title: ABACUS: Program-Guided Multistep Reasoning over Frozen Judgment Models
authors: Yuhao Wang, Zelin Zang
abstract: Judgment models answer semantic questions by scoring a finite set of candidate outcomes. Can reusable programs turn these local decisions into powerful multistep reasoning? We introduce \method, a framework that jointly constructs judgment schemas and composition programs for frozen judgment models. A generative teacher designs the procedure offline; the judgment model resolves local semantic questions online, and the saved program composes its decisions into an answer. We study three allocations of design effort between humans and the teacher, focusing on construction through a shared interface. We instantiate the framework with Kev. On three selected BIG-Bench Hard tasks, nine independently constructed programs solve all 450 executions of 150 development inputs. A separate deployment study freezes three programs after development-set reference-agreement refinement and evaluates them on 600 held-out questions. These programs achieve near-perfect 99.67\% macro accuracy, versus 64.00\% for direct Kev and 68.80\% for final-answer-only Qwen3.5-4B. They attain comparable observed accuracy to Qwen's unrestricted response policy (99.07\%) with an \textbf{8.43-fold online speedup}: 0.255 versus 2.150 seconds per question. These results show how reusable programs can substantially expand the reasoning capability of a compact judgment model while keeping its parameters fixed.

title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
authors: Zhiyu Li, Zeyu Zhang, Linyun Liu, Yiwei Bu, Chenyang Xi, Xichong Zhang, Yi Yu, Yu Yu, Zhichen Liu, Yuxiao Yi, Chunyu Li, Haoran Liu, Zhenkai Ding, Le Zhou, Juncheng Zhang, Boyu Chen, Zehao Lin, Guorui Li, Renyu Fu, Ji Li, Youyang Xia, Jiajun Shen, Harvey Li, Jinsong Zhou, Helan Hu, Tong Shen, Tianxiao Xu, Chenye Han, Weijie Li, Zhongquan Zhou, Hongming Xu, Yuekeng Li, Erenkai Zhu, Peng Yu, Wenhao Li, Jingyi Kang, Xixuan Hao, Xuzhou Zhu, Can Chen, Jiawei Liu, Chen Jiang, Tao Jiang, Fangwei Xiang, Zepeng Yao, Kai Chen, Guang Yang, Mingfei Lu, Chunhui Li, Zhengxuan Jiang, Bo Tang, Shiyu Zhan, Yihang Sun, Jie Chu, Wenjun Xiong, Zhenxiang Hua, Chen Lin, Detong Su, Dongyu Deng, Qiuping Ding, Guofeng Ding, Si Chen, Guohua Wen, Xu Chen, Zhi-Qin John Xu, Ying-Cong Chen, Ningyu Zhang, Haofen Wang, Muning Wen, Haotian Chen, Wentao Zhang, Xuanhe Zhou, Rita Zhang, Junchi Yan, Feiyu Xiong
abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano, MemT-1.0-Flash, and MemT-1.0-Pro, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
authors: Ke Zhang, Sahchit Chundur, Jerry Peprah Owusu, Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi, Maziar Raissi
abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.

title: Activation-Space Exploration for Visual and Textual Reasoning with RLVR
authors: Yunan Zeng, Jinhao Jing, Xi Cheng, Yuwang Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves visual and textual reasoning by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. Under the same rollout budget, ASE improves average accuracy over GRPO on Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct by 5.41 and 3.15 percentage points across six visual mathematical and six general visual reasoning benchmarks, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, it improves average Mean@8 over GRPO across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks by 4.87 percentage points, with gains also observed on Qwen3-8B-Base.

title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
authors: Ioannis Anagnostides, Constantinos Daskalakis, Gabriele Farina, Noah Golowich, Tuomas Sandholm, Brian Hu Zhang
abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.

title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
authors: Valentin Munteanu, Alexander Hinderhofer, Dmitry Lapkin, Vladimir Starostin, Frank Schreiber
abstract: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

title: RIPPLE: Recovery Internalization through Process-Level Policy Learning and Effect-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Agentic Coding
authors: Jingxuan Xu, Zihang Xu, Yuechen Luo, Ziqi Miao, Wenqiang Zhu, Weihao Li, Junhao Fan, Xinshun Feng, Zhiyi Lai, Yanan Wu, Haoyang Huang, Ken Deng
abstract: Long-horizon coding agents can observe a failure and generate a plausible critique yet continue along the same incorrect trajectory. We call this the Critique-to-Action Handoff Gap. We introduce RIPPLE, a recovery-oriented training framework that internalizes process-level guidance into a single self-recovering policy. A prefix-only teacher provides evidence-grounded recovery supervision without access to future actions or terminal outcomes. After lightweight distillation, reinforcement learning assigns stage-specific credit to reflection triggering, diagnosis, and corrective action. Local validity signals gate trajectory advantages so that intermediate recovery decisions do not indiscriminately inherit terminal outcomes. Across four repository-level software-engineering benchmarks, RIPPLE improves the base policy by an arithmetic mean of 4.8 score points, with no auxiliary critic at deployment. Controlled ablations isolate the benefits of local, stage-aligned credit, and matched-prefix interventions show that critique semantics affect subsequent correction. Recovery gains concentrate where the prefix contains sufficient diagnostic evidence and the repository state remains reversible within the remaining budget.

title: Not All Mislabels Are Equal: Efficient Task-Aware Auditing with Confidence Sequences
authors: Fangyuan Lin, Noah Krever, Jakub \v{C}ern\'y, Lily Xu
abstract: We study efficient, adaptive auditing of categorical labels in a fixed dataset, motivated by biodiversity credit programs in which expert verification of species records is costly and downstream scores (e.g., payment) are more sensitive to errors on certain labels than on others. Our proposed ATLAS framework couples anytime-valid inference with a task-aware adaptive auditing policy. Representing label corrections through a confusion matrix, we prioritize which data points to inspect next based on both label uncertainty and the influence of potential label corrections on the downstream score function. In our main case study on Kenyan biodiversity data, task-aware auditing reduces the expert review needed to estimate both the mislabel rate and the nonlinear biodiversity score while maintaining anytime-valid guarantees. We also evaluate ATLAS on public datasets for image classification and named-entity recognition. Across our experiments with linear and nonlinear scores, ATLAS generally reaches the same precision as competing anytime-valid methods with substantially fewer audits. When distribution-free guarantees are prohibitively costly, we develop a model-based Bayesian alternative that can further reduce the number of audits by relying on modeling assumptions. Our biodiversity case study highlights a gap between statistical validity and practical feasibility: generic methods such as Serfling's bound and existing confidence-sequence procedures are rigorous but can require prohibitively many expert reviews in practice. Together, these results show task-aware auditing can significantly reduce the number of expert audits needed while providing finite-sample, anytime-valid guarantees

title: Estimating aerosol particle number size distributions from PM2.5 with physics-regularized flow matching
authors: Zhi-Song Liu, Jenni K\"oykk\"a, Wenqing Peng, Ammar Kheder, Petri Clusius, Michael Boy
abstract: The mass concentration of particles smaller than 2.5um (PM2.5) is cheap to measure and widely monitored, whereas the particle number size distribution (PNSD) requires costly instruments and is measured at only a few research stations. Yet many aerosol effects, such as vapor uptake, cloud droplet formation and deposition in the human respiratory tract, depend on the PNSD rather than on mass. We explore whether generative deep learning models can infer the current PNSD from routine data: from the PM2.5 record and eight meteorological variables over a 24h window, a model generates an ensemble of plausible hourly PNSDs for the same window, reflecting that one mass can arise from many size distributions. Rather than proposing a single best model, we use two contrasting Finnish stations, the boreal forest site Hyytiala and the urban site Kumpula, as a controlled testbed. On it, we benchmark six generative models against deterministic regression and historical-mean baselines, locally and after transfer between sites, and test physical constraints for neural network training. Flow matching performs best overall; its guided variant has the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at both sites. A constraint based on a reduced aerosol general dynamic equation (GDE) lowers the CRPS by 5.5-11.5% at the training site and reduces errors after transfer between sites. Transfer remains harder than local estimation, identifying multi-station training as the next step towards PNSD estimates at unmonitored locations. This benchmark establishes physics-informed generative models as a promising route from routine air-quality monitoring to size-resolved aerosol information.

title: MatOS: An Agent Operating System for Materials Research
authors: Dingyang Lyu, Jing Gao, Zhonghao Chang, Jingjie Huang, Xiangran Cheng, Xin He, Yongda Huang, Zhen Lei, Zefeng Li, Jiahui Liu, Jian Wen, Feng Yu, Bonan Zhu, Yongheng Li, Hongwei Du, Baole Wei, Ziheng Lu
abstract: Materials research relies on scattered and growing data, knowledge, and simulation tools, and a single study often spans multi-day workflows across literature analysis, computation, and experiment. Large language model agents can now retrieve materials data, operate simulation codes, and close design-synthesis-characterization loops with autonomous laboratories. However, extending these agents with new capabilities, keeping long-running tasks on track, and letting them learn from past tasks and user feedback remain difficult. Here we present MatOS, an agent operating system for materials research with three core components: (1) a layered scientific asset graph that organizes data, knowledge, tools, skills, roles, and workflows as reusable assets; (2) a stateful adaptive workflow that runs tasks as explicit execution graphs with scientific checks, so that they can be resumed and traced; and (3) evidence-driven asset evolution, which revises these assets from execution records and user feedback. On ResearchClawBench, MatOS improves on the previously best-performing agent by 11.15% with the same base model and extends the cost-score Pareto frontier. With a common base model, it outperforms Codex CLI and Claude Code, exceeding Codex CLI by 2.13% on MatTools and 4.17% on SciAgentGym. In eight research cases, MatOS narrowed more than 30 million candidate structures to 97 solid-electrolyte candidates, identified 89 halide variants with higher computed conductivity than their parent structures, linked the force errors of 11 pretrained interatomic potentials to local atomic environments, and supported two new methods that reduce errors by 3.1% and 13.6% relative to their baselines. These results show that organizing research capabilities as reusable, evolving assets enables agents to carry out long, multistage materials studies. Code is available at https://github.com/DingyangLyu/MatOS.

title: Shared Context, Separate Engines: Stateful Streaming Inference for Multimodal LLMs on Edge SoCs
authors: Yilong Li, Chengpo Yan, Yijing Zeng, Hanlei Wu, Mingjun Song, Suman Banerjee
abstract:
Streaming multimodal large language models (MLLMs) must take in new video frames while answering questions about what they have already seen. On an edge SoC, if one engine does both, ingestion and answering compete for its time while the other engines sit idle. To take over a query, another engine must first import or rebuild the accumulated history, because each runtime keeps it as KV state in its own format. 
ame lets one engine answer from history that another engine built. Each query reads the history as it stood when the query was asked, so one engine can keep ingesting while another answers. The CPU and GPU can also decode answers to different queries simultaneously. Phase-level state continuation lets an engine prefill a query, pass its KV state to another engine for decoding, and return to ingestion. State-Driven Execution Planning (SDEP) chooses where each query is prefilled and decoded, based on the state each engine holds and the work queued on it. Across M4 Max, RK3588, and QCS6490, 
ame outperforms single-engine execution. On a live M4 Max stream, SDEP cuts p95 time to first token by $76\%$, and every query receives its first token within one second. Under backlog, it raises request throughput by up to $35\%$. For two concurrent video streams on RK3588, SDEP delivers $19.6\%$ higher request throughput than single-engine execution and $27.2\%$ more than running both engines in parallel without shared state. 
ame delivers up to $2.48	imes$ the throughput of the same engines run serially. Every answer matches serial execution token for token.

title: Multi-Label Agreement: A Flexible Framework for Inter-Annotator Reliability
authors: Tim Menzner, Jochen L. Leidner
abstract: Reliable evaluation of inter-annotator agreement (IAA) is important for assessing the consistency of annotation processes. While established IAA metrics such as Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa, and Krippendorff's alpha are commonly applied in single-label settings, multi-label tasks require additional decisions about how full label sets, joint selections, and joint omissions should be compared. In this work, we present Multi-Label Agreement (MLA), a flexible framework for evaluating agreement in multi-label annotation tasks. MLA preserves the full binary label vectors assigned to each item and uses average pairwise Hamming agreement, thereby accounting for both joint selections and joint omissions. Its pooled-marginal form is not a mathematically independent coefficient: it is a chance-disagreement-weighted average of label-wise Fleiss/Scott-type coefficients and is closely related to Krippendorff's alpha with normalized Hamming distance. The framework supports pooled-marginal, Gwet AC1, and fixed-baseline normalizations, yields item-level, label-level, and corpus-level results, and includes a conditional minimum-agreement diagnostic. Through a worked example and Monte Carlo simulations, we show how the resulting values depend on label prevalence, the declared label inventory, and the selected model of expected agreement. We also provide a Python implementation. MLA thus offers a transparent and interpretable framework for multi-label agreement analysis without claiming that one normalization is universally preferable.

title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
authors: Yuxi Huang, Silin Zhou, Chenhao Wang, Zihan Li, Gangming Guo, Pei Ke, Lisi Chen, Shen Gao, Shuo Shang
abstract: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We formalize item-level preference distillation on the SID prefix tree, deriving an exact factorization of item preference distributions into prefix conditionals and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into conditional KL terms. Guided by this decomposition, we renormalize the generator's probabilities over legal next tokens and match the resulting distributions to the teacher's conditional preferences along the ground-truth SID path, jointly optimizing the distillation objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation and demonstrate that REGER consistently outperforms existing GR baselines while retaining efficient inference.

title: Cassette-Editor: Shared Timeline Semantics for Human and Agent Editing
authors: Zhixin Zeng, Jiahao Zhong
abstract: Video editing involves tedious manual manipulation across interconnected timeline tracks, motivating automated agents that offload routine work while keeping the project directly revisable by humans. Fixed operation catalogs limit expressiveness, while even a basic trim requires coordinated updates across later clips, attached titles, and transitions. We present Cassette-Editor, an agent harness that unifies manual user gestures and automated agent patches within a shared editing environment. The shared action language expresses the editor's manual content changes, and a common history records committed edits for undo and manual refinement. When the model selects an edit, a state executor automatically derives its downstream consequences, such as shifting later clips and attached titles after a trim, while a validation rulebook enforces structural invariants and returns localized diagnostics for automated repair. To keep the agent grounded as the project evolves, dynamic read operations map transcripts and shot descriptions onto the current timeline. Evaluated with GPT-6 Luna, the full harness passed the scored request checks in 92/93 trials across 31 authored requests on two interview documentaries, compared with 48/93 for an internal basic-tools baseline. In ablations, disabling the consequences derived by the executor reduced passed trials from 230/232 to 199/232 on edits with dependent timeline elements, while ablating rulebook validation and repair lowered passed trials from 46/48 to 10/48 on requests operating near structural validity boundaries. Evaluating the complete system on 50 TVSum videos further demonstrated greater agreement with human annotations than a general agent using the same model (F1 23.8 vs. 20.1).

title: Alpha-TCM: Auditable Knowledge Integration for Multimodal TCM Inference
authors: Yucheng Liu, Everett X. Wang
abstract: Knowledge-guided multimodal systems need a way to measure how supplied knowledge affects predictions, including when that knowledge is wrong. Alpha-TCM addresses this problem for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) through an implemented workflow that separates measurements, supplied knowledge, predictions, and reviewer decisions. Observations and contextual knowledge enter separately, and a replaceable prior allows controlled interventions with fixed modality encoders. Bayesian committee accounting removes the reference prior already contained in each encoder before inserting contextual knowledge. A fully simulated confirmation study uses ten paired seeds and four training sizes. Knowledge context reduces prediction error relative to knowledge-free fusion at 600 and 1,200 training cases; equal-information learned context is competitive at 600 and has lower error at larger sizes. Controlled corruption identifies overconfident and displaced priors as the most damaging challenges. Case-level conflict detection remains weak, and training-time prior regularisation shows no consistent benefit. Functional tests verify the connected workflow separately from predictive performance. The simulation demonstrates how Alpha-TCM measures knowledge dependence, separates it from gains due to additional context, and exposes harmful prior assumptions before clinical evaluation.

title: Seeing Is Not Enough: Knowledge-Grounded Active Inquiry from Uncertain Visual Evidence
authors: Yucheng Liu, Everett X. Wang
abstract: Similar tongue findings can accompany different syndromes in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), with decisive symptoms absent from the photograph. We present a framework for tongue assessment in which image and pulse findings guide targeted symptom inquiry and acquired answers refine the syndrome shortlist before reporting. Image/pulse predictions guide selection from a sourced symptom question bank. Known answers update the assessment used to select the next question. A calibrated loss of support for the initial prediction triggers reassessment; a subsequent report requires fresh answers supporting a stable candidate. Question and answer records make these decisions inspectable. We construct 2,600 cases from distinct real tongue photographs, assigned syndromes, simulated symptom responses and rendered pulses; 2,599 enter five-fold source-disjoint evaluation and one is training-only. On clean images, image/pulse prediction alone achieves 46.4% fine-syndrome accuracy. At acquisition cost 12, inquiry without image/pulse evidence reaches 34.4%, whereas their combination reaches 65.8% accuracy and 90.8% top-three inclusion. A same-prior, training-optimized static order reaches 59.4% and 87.3%, respectively. In a 200-case visual-training intervention within the same bank, the first question changes in 46.7% of cases and the inquiry NLL-cost curve improves. Component comparisons distinguish these acquisition gains from the coverage-cost tradeoff of reassessment. These controlled results support image-guided acquisition of missing symptoms for ranked TCM decision support.

title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
authors: Yuhao Lu, Jiongxu Chen, Hexiang Wei, Jiajin Wu, Juelin Li, Mingjian Liang, Fan Yang, Zhuowei Liang, Zihao Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Lin Shao
abstract: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://worldflow-rbs.github.io/.

title: Formalizing the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes by a Generalized Notion of Co-dimension
authors: Ernesto Araya, Gitta Kutyniok, Weilin Li, Johannes Maly, Manjot Singh
abstract: In this work, we formalize the concept of intrinsic dimension of objective landscapes introduced in Li et al. (2018), which measures the structural complexity of learning problems by training along randomly generated subspaces. We define the intrinsic dimension of a set $\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^p$ as the minimal dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ such that a random plane of dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ intersects $\Theta$ with probability one. We show that it is a generalized notion of co-dimension that depends on the global geometry of $\Theta$. We study mathematical properties of the intrinsic dimension and develop techniques to estimate the intrinsic dimension of sets $\Theta$ that arise in learning problems. More specifically, we derive upper and/or lower bounds where $\Theta$ is the set of optimal parameters in student-teacher settings with shallow and deep ReLU networks, including finite and infinite sample cases, and with and without regularization. We discuss how our theory leads to novel types of generalization bounds, thereby showing that the intrinsic dimension is a measure of learning complexity. Our results connect techniques from seemingly different areas of machine learning research such as classification of symmetries of ReLU networks and stochastic geometry.

title: Illusory Truth or Salient Anomaly? Model-Dependent Responses to Repeated Poisoned Passages in RAG-Style Contexts
authors: Mehrdad Ghassabi, Audrina Ebrahimi, Sadra Hakim, Hamidreza Baradaran Kashani, Zahra Zojaji, Amin Milani Fard
abstract: Repeated passages in retrieved evidence may influence how language models identify misinformation, even when those passages restate a single underlying claim rather than provide independent support. We compare four instruction-tuned models on 200 claims from the BEIR SciFact test split using paired, fixed seven-document contexts. The minority condition contains one poisoned document and six non-target documents, whereas the majority condition contains the original poisoned document, five paraphrases, and one non-target document. Poison detection rates increase from 45.5% to 66.0% for Apertus-8B and from 4.0% to 15.5% for Aya-Expanse-8B, but decrease from 80.0% to 47.5% for Mistral-Nemo and from 25.0% to 9.5% for Gemma-3-12B-IT. All four paired comparisons are statistically significant. These contrasting results suggest that repeated poisoned evidence does not affect all models in the same way. One possible interpretation is that repetition makes the poisoned claim more conspicuous to some models, potentially facilitating its detection, while other models may treat repeated formulations as reinforcing evidence, potentially reducing their ability to identify the poisoned claim. Although these interpretations require further investigation, the findings highlight the importance of model-dependent responses to repeated evidence in retrieval-augmented settings.

title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
authors: Zixuan Chen, Wenyuan Jiang, Junling Wang, Mrinmaya Sachan, Yinya Huang
abstract: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given that mathematics is structured by dependencies rather than similarities, we restore this signal to both the training data and the model. We curate two underused dependency resources. We conduct the first systematic mining of 53 Lean Blueprint projects, a previously untapped corpus of 3,805 manually curated informal+formal nodes that capture rare, research-level premises absent from Mathlib4. We further pair it with the extraction of comprehensive, typed, multi-level Mathlib4 dependencies. We then introduce DAPS, a dependency-aware premise selector with a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective, and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure. DAPS reaches 78.74 Recall@16 on Mathlib4-Heldout (+11.41 over the strong selector LeanHammer) and widens the margin to 7xrecall on competition-style queries. Downstream, its selected premises raise Goedel-Prover-V2-8B Pass@4 on miniF2F-test from 49.90 to 54.03 and improve all four general-purpose LLMs on the informal IMO-ProofBench (up to +11.4% relative). Project page: https://daps-eth.github.io/.

title: Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments
authors: An-Sheng Jhang
abstract: Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) is a task- and model-dependent output protocol: repairing format does not guarantee better posterior accuracy, and requesting weights differs from reweighting an already generated candidate set. Across 31,672 planned/admitted evaluation units and 32,184 planned/admitted calls (excluding retries), we connect a frozen six-configuration cohort to exploratory scale/organization experiments and two independently preregistered post-cohort formal suites. Stage 1 retains 11 directional confirmations among 45 frozen tests; only increased post-outcome confirmation error on gpt-oss-120b exceeds its SESOI. P1 completes 1,920 terminal units: smaller response scales sharply lower operational string-match rates but increase Bayesian error. P2 completes 2,560 calls and 2,048 units: eliciting weights raises three errors by +2.75 / +2.05 / +3.88 pp, while within-generation weighting changes them by only -0.052 / -0.049 / -0.067 pp, a 42x-58x magnitude difference. Unconstrained joint generation with post-hoc normalization offers a local normalized-error improvement for three exhaustive options, without confirmed accuracy improvement. These results distinguish format validity, numerical accuracy and psychological susceptibility; a descriptive three-class behavioral spectrum organizes heterogeneity without identifying internal causes. Materials: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

title: Sampling Design and Confidence Tubes for Integral Curves on Riemannian Manifolds
authors: Xiaotian Chang, Qirui Hu, Cyrus Mostajeran
abstract: We estimate the integral curve of an unknown vector field from noisy tangent vector field on a known compact Riemannian manifold. We consider two sampling settings: independent observations at random locations that have already been collected, and a fixed response budget that allows subsequent locations to be chosen using pilot information. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the passive kernel estimator has curve error of order $n^{-2/(d+3)}$ in probability, with sample size $n$ and manifold dimension $d$. Its functional central limit theorem has a limit characterized by a linear stochastic differential equation. For active sampling, an independent pilot directs one new batch of measurements to neighborhoods of the target curve. Under localization, smoothness and design conditions, this concentration yields expected maximum curve error of order $N^{-1/2}$, including the pilot in the total response budget $N$. Both methods provide simultaneous geodesic confidence tubes with asymptotically exact coverage under mild conditions. Simulations show narrower active tubes in most reported settings, with improved small-sample coverage in some three-dimensional examples. Ocean-drifter observations illustrate mean-flow reconstruction on the sphere, and a canopy-flow LDA application uses retrospective active sampling to quantify lateral and vertical departures of local mean streamlines.

title: See, Think, Use: Diagnosing Perception and Reasoning Failures in VLMs
authors: Jiacheng Ding, Yanliang Qi, Cong Guo, Peihua Mai
abstract: We present See, Think, Use, a protocol that traces each answer of a vision-language model to perception, reasoning or the use of perception. The diagnosis shows a developer which stage to improve and directs test-time compute to the stage that fails. Benchmarks score the final answer, and an answer that rests on the image earns the same credit as a guess or a memorized prior. The protocol asks the model two extra questions per item and needs no access to its weights. A localization probe asks for a box around every instance and measures seeing, and a text-replacement probe answers from a description and measures thinking. Use is the rate at which the answer follows the model's own perception across counterfactual image pairs. The rate needs no answer labels, because the question and its prior are the same on both images. On two model families and six datasets the protocol shows that the knob that helps follows the task family. Answers follow the model's perception except on images that contradict a common prior, and asking the model to localize first repairs this failure when its boxes are right. Allocating compute by the measured stages comes close to the best uniform policy at lower cost and beats a random allocation of the same compute wherever a knob raises the short stage. We will release the code, the prompts and the per-question outputs.

title: Malware Clustering in the Wild: Taxonomy, Challenges, and Evaluation Metrics
authors: Raguvir S, Bojing Li, Prajna Bhandary, Charles Nicholas
abstract: As malware continues to grow in volume, diversity, and sophistication, clustering has emerged as a critical technique for analyzing large malware corpora. Clustering enables the discovery of structural relationships, behavioral patterns, and evolutionary trends, and is widely used to group unknown samples, infer malware family boundaries, and identify novel variants. However, existing research remains fragmented, employing a wide range of clustering techniques with no unified perspective that systematically organizes prior work or clearly identifies gaps in the literature. This survey addresses this gap by organizing previous malware clustering research into seven categories: centroid-based, hierarchical-based, density-based, distribution-based, mixed- type, fuzzy, and AI-driven approaches. In addition, this survey summarizes publicly available malware datasets commonly used in clustering research and examines the feature representations derived from these datasets. Our goal is to clarify the current landscape and outline promising avenues for future research on malware clustering, including how AI-driven methods may shape large-scale and reproducible analysis.

title: Forecasting How RLHF Responds to Reward-Model Edits Before Training
authors: Zixiao Wang, Duzhen Zhang, Xingbo Du, Dongxia Wu, Le Song
abstract: Responses with headers, lists and greater length receive high scores from reward models (RMs), and RLHF policies learn to produce these features even when true quality does not improve. Practitioners therefore edit their RMs, but they learn whether an edit works only after an RL run. We show that the response of a policy to an RM edit can be forecast before training, from samples of the current policy and the scores of the old and new RM. If we read the RM as a set of prices, the first-order theory of KL-regularized RL implies that each feature moves in proportion to its within-prompt covariance with the change in reward. We implant controlled price changes into retrained RMs under a 2^(4-1) fractional factorial design with a self-distilled placebo, run 54 RL runs from six parent policies, and fix every forecast before the runs. With the covariance predictor, we predict the direction of all 20 changes in supply whose forecast has the same sign at every parent and explain 82% of the standardized change. With counterfactual prices, the classical alternative, we explain 50%. The forecast also holds under GRPO and for real RM upgrades, where we explain 66% out of sample with a coefficient frozen from the factorial runs. For rent, the gap between the proxy reward and a gold reward from stronger judges, we rank RM edits correctly with the same covariance over the first 30 steps (Spearman 0.94). This measures the horizon of the forecast: by step 200, the ranking of the factorial edits reverses under both RLOO and GRPO, while the real upgrades keep their order. When we vary the KL coefficient beta, the initial response does not depend on beta, and the response saturates below the KL equilibrium. In one experiment, the long-run response to a price rise is consistent with an additional implicit regularizer beta_0 of about 0.003 to 0.007.

title: Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment
authors: Xiaopeng Mao, Morten M{\o}rup, Xin Xu, Sang Wan Lee, Sadasivan Puthusserypady
abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text interfaces offer alternative communication pathways for people with communication disabilities. However, sentence-level decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging. We propose a hierarchical EEG-text alignment framework that retrieves previously unseen sentences by progressively decoding coarse-grained semantic information and fine-grained sentence representations. We hypothesize that broader semantic context can be more reliably captured from EEG than individual sentences. Accordingly, EEG representations are first classified into semantic classes, which are defined as groups of related sentences, followed by sentence retrieval within the predicted class. Among over 2,000 unique text samples, our approach achieves, on unseen sentences, average top-5 and top-10 retrieval accuracies of 62.6\% $\pm$ 1.0\% and 83.5\% $\pm$ 1.0\%, respectively, compared with 0.3\% $\pm$ 0.3\% and 0.5\% $\pm$ 0.2\% for direct EEG-sentence alignment without semantic classification. Qualitative analysis further reveals that decoding performance depends strongly on textual context. These findings demonstrate the potential of hierarchical semantic alignment for advancing sentence-level EEG-to-text decoding.

title: Enhancing Stock Market Information Retrieval with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Huan Phong Thai, Thu Anh Ngoc Le, Nhu Huynh Thi Le, Nhan Huu Tran, Lenh Cong Phan Pham, Hong Nhung Nguyen
abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been widely applied in financial domains, enabling automated analysis and retrieval of stock market information. However, traditional NLP-based systems often struggle with maintaining contextual accuracy and generating relevant responses in dynamic financial environments. To address these challenges, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have emerged as a powerful solution, combining retrieval-based methods with generative capabilities to enhance response quality. In this study, we present a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to generate responses related to stock market information. The system integrates retrieval-based and generative approaches to enhance the accuracy and relevance of financial text generation. To evaluate its effectiveness, we employ the ROUGE metric, specifically ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, to measure lexical and structural similarity between generated and reference texts. Experimental results on a dataset of 100 stock market-related queries demonstrate high ROUGE scores, indicating strong alignment with reference documents. Additionally, we assess latency to evaluate the system responsiveness, achieving an average response time of 1.16 seconds. These findings confirm that our RAG model is capable of providing accurate and timely stock market insights, making it a promising approach for financial information retrieval.

title: Skill erosion, individual memory and the reversibility of AI adoption
authors: Renaud Lambiotte
abstract: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills needed for future work. We consider a population of agents who perform a task either with their own skill or with the help of AI. Agents tend to imitate more successful peers, and their skills evolve in time: improving with practice and eroding with reliance on AI. We study, analytically and with simulations, the collective consequences of AI adoption. We show that the mechanism of skill erosion makes adoption bistable and that the long-term behaviour of the population depends on how skills are distributed: populations with the same adoption and mean skill can reach opposite asymptotic states, depending on how expertise is shared between AI users and non-users. A deterministic description that follows the mean skills of the two groups and the variance of skills among non-users predicts the outcome of individual runs as accurately as the simulations allow, whereas the means alone are not sufficient. We also consider the situation when the benefit of AI improves in time. In that case, adoption can jump abruptly, and a temporary increase in benefit, such as in a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its original value. Skill erosion therefore creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

title: NovoCRF: Globally Normalized De Novo Peptide Sequencing on a Prefix-Mass Lattice
authors: Rui Qiao, Lei Xin, Baozhen Shan
abstract: De novo peptide sequencing has moved from dynamic programming over hand-designed or generative scores to large transformers that learn the task end to end. We present NovoCRF, a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so that its paths are exactly the peptides within $\pm$0.06 Da of the precursor mass. A small network scores each edge from physics-derived ion-match features and is trained with its scores globally normalized over all mass-feasible peptides. To our knowledge, NovoCRF is the first de novo method trained with exact normalization over all mass-feasible peptides. Our model has 3.6M parameters and trains in about 27 GPU-hours. Because it is small, NovoCRF can also adapt to each run at inference time: it fine-tunes part of its weights on the run's own confident answers, recalibrates the run's precursor and fragment masses, and uses retention time, predicted with a pretrained indexed-retention-time model, as further evidence. On nine held-out data-dependent acquisition datasets, NovoCRF has the highest peptide recall on five, and the transformer model InstaNovo on the other four. Where the spectrum determines the peptide, on labels with at most one peptide bond without a b or y ion, NovoCRF outperforms RNovA, $\pi$-PrimeNovo and CasanovoV5 on every dataset and InstaNovo on six of nine. The transformer models lead where many fragment ions are missing, and there their recall is up to 29 points higher on peptides of their own training data than on other peptides, while NovoCRF's recall differs least between seen and unseen peptides. NovoCRF also searches modifications it was never trained on at their exact mass: on a public spike-in of peptides with non-natural residues it finds 69.2% of the labeled spectra, against 64.4% for RNovA. With a GPU it sequences 203 spectra/s in its default two passes, and on the CPU alone it still sequences 67 spectra/s.

title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
authors: Ehud Shapiro
abstract: AI's inflection point is a fountain of risks for digital platforms, as those in control of global platforms cede control of the algorithms, membership and content to AI: (i) AI control of global platforms used by the majority of humanity; (ii) unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals; and (iii) unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, which people cannot distinguish from genuine content. Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon: a social contract that can be freely adopted by any group of people, where groups bound by the same contract can union by mutual consent, possibly into a single global union. Grassroots contracts are realised by grassroots platforms, person-to-person platforms owned, operated and governed by their participants. We developed, with AI, a methodology to compile grassroots contracts to working smartphone apps. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two, and show how they corral these risks: (i) grassroots platforms are not controlled by a third party who may cede control to AI; (ii) AI agents are introduced with accountability: similarly to cars, their manufacturers are accountable for manufacturing defects and their operators for reckless operation; and (iii) every item carries the signatures of its author and of every agent that forwarded it, so creators and forwarders of harmful content are accountable and culpable. Much work remains for grassroots apps to be competitive with incumbent global platforms; but perhaps now this could be achieved with some AI-months rather than with incalculably-many person-years.

title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL
authors: Mingzhe Zheng, Yue Wu, Jing Tan, Chang Zou, Dengyang Jiang, Zeyue Tian, Xuanhua He, Ryan Xu, Yunyang Ge, Sihui Ji, Yunlong Lin, Kaihang Pan, Hongru Yan, Sixiang Chen, Dianyi Wang, Julian Zhang, Weijie Kong, Changlin Li, Lanqing Guo, Zhao Zhong, Qifeng Chen, Harry Yang
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
authors: Xiaobo Chen, Genliang Zhu, Ziyuan Wang, Chu Wang
abstract: Enterprise AI agents split requests across subagents, and each handoff can drop, alter or ignore a requirement. A preregistered study on synthetic, exactly scorable tasks compares free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs it and deterministically verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no detectable utility loss versus structured handoffs (S2 -0.4 pp, 95% CI [-14.2, 13.3]). Signing defeats in-transit mutation: unsigned manifests violated 79.2 pp more often than signed ones, which never did; this replicated in gpt-oss-20b and gemma-4-12b. There, without an adversary, signed manifests were descriptively slightly worse than structured handoffs (11.1% vs 2.8%; 16.7% vs 8.3%; not tested) and lost utility overall (gpt-oss-20b, all threats: -28.7 pp). On identical Qwen3-8B trajectories, the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, and an oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits, so the residual risk is in extraction. A preregistered pre-signing injection confirmed this: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest unsafe commits from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 16.7% to 97.2% (gemma-4-12b), and every such commit carried a manifest corrupted before signing. Signing protects transit; extraction is the trust boundary. A testable pre-signing specification (PSE), specified after the injection results and frozen before an offline evaluation, blocked all these injected commits (fixed templates) but refused 45.8%, 11.1% and 22.2% of benign requests, changing completions by -8.3 pp, -2.8 pp and 0.0 pp.

title: Continued Training of Continuous Language Flows with Token Identity Squared Supervision
authors: Jiawei Jiang, Zhaoxiang Zang, Zhengtao Yu
abstract: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. When continuous predictions are formed by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities, different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under a continuous reconstruction objective based on mean squared error (MSE). We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF) to apply squared supervision directly to token identities. TIBF fixes token embeddings, combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. We show that, for fixed token embeddings, the squared error in token posterior prediction controls the squared errors of the continuous denoising prediction and the flow velocity. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, TIBF achieves mean Gen.PPL values of 34.87 on OWT and 80.08 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE controls. Further evaluations show improvements across multiple sampling budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/Jiangjiawei-kust/TIBF.

title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games
authors: Eduardo C. Garrido-Merch\'an
abstract: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison

title: Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
authors: Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose
abstract: Robots increasingly plan by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences. We measure what this search does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic and blind human labels, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76% while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97; with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs, against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from. The effect persists with a learned dynamics model and an image scorer. We prove that $\chi^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, and that no gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own. Calibrated from 100 ranked proposal pairs, this rule is the safest fix we test, keeping 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on drawer-open and plate-slide.

title: LEGIT: Live Eligibility Gating over Identifier Tries for Constrained Decoding of Heterogeneous Pages
authors: Felix Fang, Zheng Liu, Robert Saliba
abstract: A generative recommender names each candidate with a short token sequence, a Semantic ID, and recommends by generating those tokens. Some generative recommenders, including the Uber Eats search engine we are building, write a whole results page, stores with their menu items, in one decoding pass. Every Semantic ID on such a page must name a real store or item that is eligible for the search, such as a store that delivers to the user's location, and that is not already on the page. Each item must also belong to the store above it. A trie over the catalog keeps identifiers real, but eligibility and repetition change with every request and token, and the grammar-constrained decoder we tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly. We call this constraint LEGIT, for live eligibility gating over identifier tries. Numbering trie leaves depth first turns each rule into a range lookup over one store trie and one item trie, and every generated page passes an independent catalog check. On one NVIDIA B200 GPU with one or two requests per decode step, a direct implementation that walks the trie on the GPU makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding. Across 36 implementations, hardware counters and ablations are consistent with kernel launches and CPU-GPU waits as the source of this slowdown. Our fastest implementation walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model, needs no custom kernel, and cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against the direct GPU implementation, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost. This implementation is also the fastest on a page layout that puts each item before its store.

title: Regularization Amplifies Subliminal Learning
